New Scientist July 16, 2026

Stealth bombers use exotic materials to lower their radar signature and spy satellites orbit Earth far outside human sight, but a new drone avoids detection in an altogether simpler way: spinning so fast that it blurs into the background.

Emma Alexander and her colleagues at Northwestern University in Illinois created the drone, known as Phantom Twist. It spins at 25 revolutions a second to hide itself in a motion blur like the blades of a fan. But unlike a fan, which has fixed parts that remain clearly visible – the central axle, controls, a stand – every single part of Phantom Twist whirs in circles.

The unusual single-motor design was chosen through a complex, multi-stage and entirely automated process. First, an AI created a list of millions of designs, which was whittled down to around 20,000 that were theoretically able to fly.

Advertisement

Next, a second AI slightly tweaked the placement of each component in every design to minimise visibility from all viewing angles, on average. Finally, a third AI model that mimicked human sight assessed the visibility of each shortlisted design in front of various backgrounds. The researchers simply stepped in at the end to build the best, final design.

That winning design spread the components around so that none visually overlapped when spinning. The drone is small enough to fit in the palm of the hand and weighs just 30 grams.

“The motion blur essentially turns all of the mechanical components into this slight haze,” says Alexander. “And if you’re not paying attention, you might really miss that slight change in the brightness of the environment.”

David Whitaker at Cardiff University, UK, who studies optical perception, says that although the human visual system can detect changes up to 60 times a second in some situations, such as when observing a flashing LED, this rotating drone is moving fast enough that the brain simply merges its parts and the background together – not becoming invisible, but blurring enough that it can be missed if the background closely matches the drone’s colour.

“Imagine a cooling fan, spinning round and round. If it spins fast enough, you lose appreciation of the blades. The visual system can’t cope,” says Whitaker. “When things are moving fast, the visual system merges those moving objects with the background, so they become relatively invisible.”

Peter Lee at the University of Portsmouth, UK, who wasn’t involved in the research, says that stealthy drone technology has obvious military applications, but that this design – while deploying a nifty optical illusion – has serious limitations.

The trick relies on a very spindly and sparse design, so adding any additional sensors or payloads would make it more visible, he says. And adding weight or scaling the design up in size would also lead to much higher centrifugal forces, potentially making flight impossible or causing the drone to break apart. Added to this, the gyroscopic effect of a spinning drone would make quick changes of direction extremely difficult.

“This style of drone is not manoeuvrable in the way that quadcopters are highly manoeuvrable. So because of the rotation, it won’t be able to bank at steep angles,” says Lee. “It would slow the speed of the rotation, and therefore it would become more visible and it’s probably getting unstable.”

Fully autonomous drones have killed human soldiers for the first time

The researchers admit that the drone isn’t highly steerable – it can currently only hold a steady hover – and that it can still be heard easily even if not seen. But they believe that choosing transparent components rather than opaque ones, such as the black carbon-fibre rods that make up the structure, could further reduce visibility. And changes to the AI design process to take into account the visibility of even the smallest components on the device could also bring further gains.

The researchers will present their work at the Robotics: Science and Systems conference in Sydney, Australia on 16 July.

Using AI for creative pursuits? Moderation is key

New Scientist July 17, 2026

“Mischa’s parents are hosting their daughter’s engagement party at their country mansion. As she makes a toast, her wine glass slips from her hand to reveal an object embedded in the stem – a tiny memory card. The discovery unravels a decades-old corruption scandal involving her own family, forcing her to choose between justice and loyalty.”

Take control of your brain’s master switch to optimise how you think

Not bad, I suppose. I have just asked ChatGPT to create a series of concepts for a movie, based on the creative writing prompt “Her face went still as her eyes widened, watching the glass shatter on the floor”, and this is one of its better suggestions. My aim is to develop a short outline of a plot within 30 minutes.

No, I don’t have any serious aspirations to break into Hollywood. But I wanted to test out the findings of a recent paper by Hsuan-Che Brad Huang during his PhD at the University of British Columbia in Canada. There has been a lot of online discussion about whether algorithms will replace human brainwork, but Huang wanted to see whether AI can enhance our own creativity – and the answer depends on how much we use it. Too little or too much and our thinking suffers. In the “Goldilocks zone”, however, it can inspire new ideas that we might have never considered by ourselves, while leaving us with a satisfying sense of ownership over the work we have produced. Sadly, I find it highly unlikely that my experiment has produced the next blockbuster, but it has helped clarify my thoughts about the nature of creativity.

Advertisement

First, the theory. Huang’s hypothesis was based on the fact that human creativity is often constrained by our experience; we all carry certain assumptions that will direct our thinking in one direction, and so it can often be useful to hear from other ways of seeing the world. There is evidence that is why teams are often more creative than individuals. But AI could also be a tool for getting a different perspective.

The technology has its limits, of course. LLMs, which are in essence statistical tools, often present a kind of “average response” to questions, without the amazing idiosyncrasies of the human brain, and they often absorb biases and prejudices from their training data. Worse still, they can undermine our own feelings of competence, producing a kind of apathy.

For these reasons, Huang suspected that moderation was key. In much the same way that Goldilocks had to find the porridge that was neither too hot, nor too cold, we should look for a medium level of engagement that is “just right”, he argued – and he assessed the idea in a series of experiments.

Free newsletter

The first involved a classic test of creativity, in which around 150 participants were asked to assist a student named Mike in coming up with an impromptu business, given just $10 of seed funding. They were encouraged to first generate multiple ideas, before sending Mike an email setting out the best proposal in detail.

During this process, some participants were encouraged to use ChatGPT just one time, while others were recommended to employ around four to six prompts. The rest were told to use the AI at least nine times – a very high level of engagement for a 15-minute task. All participants AI at some point. Their final ideas were then assessed by expert human judges on novelty, utility and business value.

The results were exactly as Huang had predicted, with higher average scores among the participants in the middle group. To confirm the finding, he performed a second experiment with a further 319 participants, finding the same results.

Finally, he took the idea to professional creatives, through a survey of fashion designers, visual artists, authors, animators, technologists and influencers. In a questionnaire, the participants had to rate statements such as “I use artificial intelligence to carry out most of my job functions” on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). Based on their bosses’ assessments, he found that those who reported moderate use of AI (around 4 or 5 on the scale) had the most creative ideas, just as his previous experiments had suggested.

During my little experiment, I could easily see the advantage. I first asked the chatbot to think up 10 different ideas in diverse genres, before picking my favourite: the concealed memory card that is released by Mischa’s glass breaking. I built on that idea by describing what I felt would be contained on the card – a series of stills from Mischa’s grandparents’ wedding – and asked the AI to offer a continuation of the plot. It suggested that the pictures contained an elegant young woman who had been erased from all the other wedding photos.

With my remaining four prompts, we explored who the woman was (a great aunt) and why she had been “disappeared” (she had witnessed her brother, Mischa’s grandfather, committing a crime). The showdown, we decided, would occur at Mischa’s own wedding.

At each stage, the AI helped broaden the range of events that I was considering, but I had to use my human mind to keep the story coherent and to create some kind of narrative arc. This almost certainly helped me come up with a more intricate plot than I could have possibly managed on my own in the time that I had. But I still have reservations.

How I used psychology to come back from the worst year of my life

It isn’t just the ethical issues I would have in trying to pass off an AI collaboration as my own work, and the risk of plagiarising others’ work through the algorithm’s suggestions, but what I think is lost when we outsource our thinking. I’ve recently started dabbling in writing short fiction, and I love the sensation of my synapses straining to find new connections, and the genuine sense of surprise when new motifs and themes emerge unexpectedly, connected, in some way, to my personal experience and the emotions that I am feeling. All of that was lost in this experiment.

Perhaps most seriously, I am worried about what the employment of AI might do to my long-term development. In a recent study, currently under peer review, Grace Liu at Carnegie Mellon University in Pennsylvania and her colleagues have shown that people quickly become reliant on AI and less persistent in the absence of the technology. I doubt this is a permanent change, but still – I hate the thought that I am somehow setting myself up for lazy thinking in the future. Writing, for me, should be a continual learning curve.

This isn’t to judge anyone who does choose to create with AI. I am sure many people can do so without stunting their intellect. But if genius really does involve more perspiration than inspiration, as the famous saying claims, I’d much prefer to sweat it out myself.

David Robson’s latest book is The Laws of Connection: 13 social strategies that will transform your life. If you have a question that you would like answered in his column, please send him a message at davidrobson. me/contact

Supplement that binds to microplastics may remove them from our body

New Scientist July 17, 2026

A postbiotic may limit our absorption of microplastics, according to the first human trial of a microplastic-removal supplement. It uses the rough surface of dead bacteria to attract microplastics, preventing them from entering cells.

Microplastics, which are less than 5 millimetres long, are ubiquitous in the environment and have been detected throughout the human body. Research has shown that people with arterial plaques containing microplastics are more than four times as likely to have a heart attack or stroke than those with plastic-free plaques. Higher concentrations of microplastics have also been reported in the brains of people with Alzheimer’s disease. However, neither finding proves that microplastics cause these conditions.

How worried should you be about microplastics?

“We don’t really know what microplastics do, but we do know they don’t belong in the human body,” says Eva Berkes, co-founder and chief scientific officer at Quorum Innovations in Florida, the biopharmaceutical company that developed the postbiotic, a supplement made from the parts or byproducts of dead bacteria. “If we have a reasonably safe and fairly inexpensive way of modifying [potential] risks, then maybe we shouldn’t wait 20 years for a more conclusive answer before we do that.”

Advertisement

Berkes and her team created the postbiotic, called Qi601, by growing the bacterium Limosilactobacillus fermentum, killing it with heat and collecting its cell walls. They then incubated microplastics and Qi601 together and found the plastic particles stuck to the walls’ rough surfaces.

Free newsletter

To gauge whether this would work in the body, they added nanoplastics – smaller than 0.001 millimetres – and Qi601 to fluids resembling different parts of the digestive system and found that up to 92 per cent of them spontaneously bound to the postbiotic.

The researchers also exposed human intestinal-like cells to nanoplastics with and without the postbiotic and found that when Qi601 wasn’t present, nanoplastics accumulated within cells and on their surfaces. When Qi601 was added, significantly less nanoplastics were visible inside or on the cells, suggesting that the postbiotic mopped them up before they could be absorbed.

In another part of the experiment, the researchers wanted to see whether Qi601 could remove nanoplastics already inside cells. They first exposed cells to nanoplastics in the lab for 24 hours and later added Qi601, which reduced the number of plastic particles inside the cells by 43 per cent. This seems to happen by Qi601 capturing plastic when it is transported in and out of cells during a process called vesicle recycling.

Finally, participants chewed commercial gum, which releases numerous microplastic particles into saliva, until they had collected 10 millilitres of saliva. The researchers then repeated the experiment but placed 10 milligrams of powdered Qi601 in the participants’ mouths after 5 seconds of chewing. Analysis of the saliva from one participant showed 2152 freely floating plastic particles after chewing gum alone, compared with 185 when Qi601 was added.

“Our results represent the first demonstration of microplastics being bound by a microplastic mitigant in [people],” says Berke. However, the study hasn’t shown that the particles were prevented from entering cells in the human gut or that they were excreted. The team also notes that the results could be affected by the presence of food, immune cells or the complex architecture of the gut.

Martin Wagner at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology also points out that people are constantly exposed to microplastics through food, water and air. “[The postbiotic] would not remove the inhaled particles, a major source of exposure, nor would it address the continuous nature of exposure,” he says. “Reducing these exposures at the source is much more efficient in protecting health, rather than trying to remove plastic particles from the body retrospectively.”

bioRxiv DOI: 10.64898/2026.05.11.724280

Why a Ukrainian cruise missile is flying with hobby drone hardware

New Scientist July 17, 2026

Ukraine has developed a cheap cruise missile guided by an open-source autopilot system typically found in consumer drones. The use of hobby components highlights the shrinking gap between military and consumer electronics, which may make it easier for small countries and non-state actors to develop powerful high-tech weapons.

With foreign long-range weapons hard to come by, Ukraine has had to develop its own. Fire Point, a Ukrainian company, showed off its FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile at the Eurosatory defence expo in Paris last month. The 6-tonne missile can carry a warhead twice as heavy as a Tomahawk cruise missile for twice the distance, but costs a fraction as much.

Fully autonomous drones have killed human soldiers for the first time

One secret of Flamingo’s low cost is its Ardupilot flight controller, which uses sensor data to keep the missile flying stably along its assigned path.

Advertisement

Ardupilot is an open-source software suite that has been around since 2009, and can run on hardware costing less than $100. Drone hobbyists use Ardupilot on everything from multicopters and model aircraft to boats and ground vehicles.

In a post on X, Fire Point’s Chief Technology Officer Iryna Terekh said open-source software offers independence because it doesn’t come from a company that may go out of business or be blocked from exporting to Ukraine. What’s more, a community of thousands of engineers quickly finds and resolves bugs in the software.

Free newsletter

“The use of open-source Ardupilot is in keeping with Fire Point’s whole philosophy of rapidly providing effective long-range strike at a vastly lower cost than exquisite Western designs,” says Roy Gardiner at the non-profit group Defense Tech for Ukraine.

Gardiner notes that Ardupilot is one the world’s most extensively tested autopilots. Ukraine’s vast fleet of small drones, many derived from hobby designs, runs largely on open-source flight controllers such as Betaflight, Ardupilot and PX4.

Russia is also relying heavily on commercial electronics in its Shahed attack drones, according to Ukrainian drone expert Serhii Beskrestnov. Waves of Shaheds hit Ukraine every night, and while earlier versions navigated by satellite, a new “Seeker” version has a camera and Raspberry Pi 4 processor with AI software to lock on to targets, Beskrestnov said on Telegram. The Raspberry Pi, made in the UK, is used in educational and hobby computing projects.

How Ukraine became a drone factory and invented the future of war

The software on the Shahed hasn’t been identified, but smaller drones often use Raspberry Pi with open-source vision software called YOLO for locking on to targets.

Ukraine has also deployed the more conventional Storm Shadow cruise missiles developed by French and British companies, while Russia has its own high-end Kalibr cruise missiles.

But given the rapid improvement in commercial hardware and open-source software in recent decades, it is unclear how well these legacy systems, with their high costs but arguably superior performance, can compete in the long run. “Over time, expensive custom military electronics and software will likely be developed only for the most demanding requirements,” says Gardiner.

Now, small countries can produce weapons almost as capable as those of their large, well-funded neighbours, and non-state actors can make their own cruise missiles. “The dramatic reduction in cost gives many state and non-state actors access to strike capabilities that were previously available only to the wealthiest nations,” says Gardiner.

Why the upcoming eclipse is still vital in the age of solar probes

New Scientist July 17, 2026

Western Europe’s first total solar eclipse since 1999 will happen on 12 August and see eclipse chasers travel to eastern Greenland, western Iceland and northern Spain for totality, when the moon covers the sun’s disc and the usually hidden solar corona bursts into view. Solar and atmospheric scientists will be among them – and above them.

It is tempting to think total solar eclipses have been made obsolete for scientists by spacecraft. NASA’s Parker Solar Probe has flown through the sun’s corona, while the European Space Agency’s Solar Orbiter and NASA’s Solar and Heliospheric Observatory study the sun from space. ESA’s Proba-3 mission can even create artificial eclipses in orbit. So why do scientists still need to chase the moon’s shadow across Earth?

The answer is simple: total eclipses offer cheap and accessible opportunities to study both the sun and Earth. “Research groups that have novel ideas can go to an eclipse and take observations without having to bid for tens of millions of pounds’ worth of grants from NASA or the European Space Agency – the barrier to entry is much lower,” says Ryan French, a solar physicist at the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics in Boulder, Colorado.

Advertisement

Where, when and how to watch the 2026 solar eclipse

One example is the Nationwide Eclipse Ballooning Project, which will send teams from several US universities to Spain and Iceland to study atmospheric responses to the eclipse. Balloons released in Spain will reach an altitude of 27 to 37 kilometres, carrying 360-degree cameras, ozone instruments and radio experiments. Icelandic teams will launch balloons carrying radiosondes, devices that can monitor pressure, temperature, humidity and other atmospheric parameters. The idea is to measure the effects the eclipse has on the planetary boundary layer, the atmosphere’s lowest region where its behaviour is most heavily influenced by warm air rising from the ground.

NASA’s WB-57 high-altitude aircraft can measure polarised coronal light and will fly for the 2026 eclipse. Flying high avoids the problem of cloud cover obscuring the view, while also minimising atmospheric interference. “At high altitude, you can observe infrared light that you can’t observe from the ground,” says French.

During the 2024 total solar eclipse, Citizen CATE – an experiment funded by the US National Science Foundation and NASA – used telescopes spread along the path of totality to create a 1-hour timelapse of the corona. This will be repeated during the 2026 eclipse, ahead of a plan to produce a timelapse of the corona with the larger North African Telescope Eclipse experiment during the longer eclipse that will happen in August 2027. Totality in 2027 will last much longer because the new moon will be closer to Earth, and the path of totality is close to the equator, where Earth effectively bulges out towards the moon.

Subscriber-only newsletter

“Most of the scientific instruments at an eclipse are not just taking photographs, but collecting measurements of spectra,” says French. Spectroscopy can reveal the speed, temperature and density of plasma in the corona. “When you observe specific spectra, this can give you information on the speed of plasma moving in the sun, and can tell you about the temperature and the density of plasma sloshing around the sun,” he says.

Other eclipse scientists ask a fundamental question: what is the radius of the sun? Because the sun has no solid surface, its visible edge is difficult to define. Yet tiny differences can shift the predicted edge of the path of totality. The Besselian Elements Team, a group of researchers scattered across the world, records flash spectra at the path’s edge to refine eclipse maps and calculate the sun’s actual radius.

The eclipse may also offer a rare chance to test whether aurora can be detected during totality. NASA scientist Liz MacDonald, founder of citizen science project Aurorasaurus, will use all-sky cameras to search for faint auroral glow. It is a long shot, but Iceland lies beneath the auroral oval, a region surrounding the geomagnetic North Pole within which the aurora can regularly be seen. Even a non-detection could help constrain whether eclipse darkness can reveal aurora.

Total solar eclipses are brief, vulnerable to clouds and geographically specific, but they open a rare observing window onto the sun’s inner corona – and let scientists try bold ideas without first building a spacecraft.

Ancient Egyptian princesses buried with weapons may have been fighters

New Scientist July 17, 2026

Ancient Egyptian princesses were probably trained in using bows and daggers and put themselves at risk of serious injury. Rediscovering mummies from about 3800 years ago has revealed that some of these women had enlarged bones in their arms and bowing of the bones in their palms, which suggests they were active users of the weapons they were often buried with.

“They carried their bows and daggers into the afterlife not just as ornaments, but as testaments to the active, resilient and powerful lives they led,” says Zeinab Hashesh at Beni-Suef University in Egypt.

Archaeologists are unearthing the most powerful women who ever lived

Weapons have been found buried with women from many cultures throughout history. But there has been much debate about whether this was symbolic or meant the women used them.

Advertisement

Now, Hashesh and her colleagues have studied six royal mummies – five female – found at the Dahshur complex of pyramids and tombs from Egypt’s Middle Kingdom between about 1850 and 1700 BC. The mummies, some of which were found with bows and arrows alongside them, were excavated in the 1890s, and were rediscovered in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo during a curation project in 2020.

The team has analysed the bones to learn about the lives of these royal individuals, four of whom are thought to be daughters of the pharaoh Amenemhat II.

A key finding was that Princess Ita – who had an elaborate gold and lapis lazuli dagger in her burial assemblage and was aged between 28 and 34 when she died – would have had very strong connections between the bones in her forearm and strong hand muscles. This implies the habitual gripping of weapons like daggers or maces, says Hashesh.

Princesses Noub-Hotep (aged between 40 and 44) and Itaweret (aged 20 to 34) both showed enlargement of the radius bone in the forearm, which could be an adaptation to the repetitive stress of drawing a bow. The former princess, who was buried alongside arrows, also had bowing of the second right metacarpal bone in the palm and strengthened attachments of finger muscles. These hint at the sustained mechanical load required to hold a bow and are indicative of “archer’s grip”.

“I imagine the lives of princesses like Noub-Hotep and Ita were far from the sedentary, purely decorative existence we often associate with ancient royalty,” says Hashesh. “To develop the archer’s grip and the structural bowing of the hand bones observed in Noub-Hotep, they must have begun training in archery and martial arts from a young age.”

Michelle Langley at Griffith University in Australia says this study gives us real insight into these princesses’ lives. “Royal women were not simply sitting around a palace or following their menfolk around, but living active and skilled lives. They were trained in very practical martial and hunting arts, just as we imagine their fathers and brothers were,” she says.

Treasures from sunken Egyptian city of Canopus emerge from the sea

The bones also revealed that injuries were common. For example, Princess Itaweret survived broken ribs and foot fractures, which Hashesh says were probably caused by accidents or hard blows.

“This tells us that they were out in the world, perhaps engaged in high-impact activities where falls and blows were a real danger,” she says. When injured, their status gave them access to surgeons capable of setting bones so well that they healed without infection or misalignment, she says.

But Sonia Zakrzewski at the University of Southampton, UK, says that other activities could result in similar alterations to arm and hand bones, such as frequent juggling or using a scythe. “If we were to find a tennis player buried with a club, we cannot simply argue that this [similar] bony change was a result of clubbing people,” she says.

Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology DOI: 10.3389/fearc.2026.1844402

Waikato ambulance officer Matthew Liddle dies after months-long fight for life following brain aneurysm

New Zealand Herald July 18, 2026

Matthew Liddle died on Friday following a seizure which caused catastrophic brain pressure. Photo / Givealittle

An ambulance officer who died from a “catastrophic” seizure has been remembered as a devoted husband and father who cared for everyone he met.

Waikato-based Matthew Liddle suffered a brain aneurysm around six months ago. He died in the early hours of Friday after experiencing a massive seizure during his recovery.

His family announced the death on a Givealittle page.

“The fight is over. Rest easy my Love”, his wife Danielle Liddle wrote.

She said he was taken to the intensive care unit after contracting another infection in his brain fluid.

“He had a seizure which caused catastrophic brain pressure. Matthew would not be able to come back from this.”

Liddle worked as an emergency medical technician and was in his final year of studies to become a qualified paramedic.

The page said he was born with heart defects and had multiple open-heart operations.

The last surgery involved a mechanical heart valve, which required lifelong blood-thinning medication and monitoring.

Around six months ago, he had a brain aneurysm which caused “a massive bleed in the back of the brain”.

The blood thinners meant the bleed progressed rapidly.

Since then, family members have been sharing updates about his journey.

Some described signs of recovery, with a post in March saying he had come a long way and was feeling positive.

Other updates mentioned the emotional toll of the injury and setbacks he faced through infections.

More than $37,000 has been donated to the page, which was made to help cover living expenses, travel to and from the hospital, childcare needs and other costs after his aneurysm.

A social media tribute from Hato Hone St John Cambridge said Liddle started with the ambulance service as a cadet before moving into volunteer work in Te Aroha, where he remained living with his family.

“Matthew was a highly respected emergency medical technician at Matamata Station. He started his paid career with St John in Cambridge.

“He will be remembered for the kindness, compassion, and genuine care he showed to his patients, colleagues, and everyone he met.”

Liddle brought a positive outlook to those around him and made a lasting impact on the communities he served, the post said.

The Givealittle page said Liddle did not have life insurance and asked for donations to help with funeral costs.

He is survived by his wife and young son.

High antidepressant script numbers highlight crisis in youth mental health

New Zealand Herald July 18, 2026

Experts warn the drugs come with an increased risk of suicidal thoughts, and young people are not being monitored properly after being prescribed them. Photo / 123rf

Antidepressants are increasingly becoming the first-line treatment for thousands of young New Zealanders, as an over-stretched mental health system leaves doctors with few other options, experts warn.

Data obtained by the Herald under the Official Information Act (OIA) reveals tens of thousands of children and young adults were dispensed the medications last year.

Antidepressants play an important role in treating severe depression and can be lifesaving in the most serious cases, experts say. But clinicians spoken to by the Herald stressed they should be paired with therapy rather than used as a standalone solution.

Experts warn that in some cases, the drugs come with an increased risk of suicidal thoughts, and young people are often not being properly monitored.

This comes amid growing debate over social media’s role in youth mental health, with experts warning the platforms are complicating an already strained system.

The OIA data shows 5481 children aged 10 to 14 were dispensed selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) in 2025. The number rises to 23,727 among 15- to 19-year-olds and 34,272 among those aged 20 to 24.

The figures also highlight a marked rise over the past decade. In 2016, 12,617 people aged 14 to 18 were dispensed SSRIs, nearly half the number recorded among 15- to 19-year-olds last year.

Clinical psychologist Kyle MacDonald said antidepressants were increasingly becoming the frontline treatment for young people out of necessity rather than best practice, as growing demand for mental health support collided with a lack of funded services.

MacDonald said antidepressants were not recommended as the first-line treatment for adolescents.

“Some SSRIs, such as Prozac and Aropax, can have side effects for some young people, specifically increasing suicidal ideation, so if they’re prescribed it should be done under reasonably close supervision,” he said.

“In an ideal world, counselling and therapy should be where we start, particularly with adolescents, but more generally with anyone struggling with mild to moderate depression.”

MacDonald said the medication should be used in serious cases, but counselling and therapy remained essential, alongside any medication.

“As a rough guide, for mild to moderate depression, therapy first and medication if therapy’s not getting much traction, and for severe depression both right from the get-go.”

New Zealand had seen a well-established increase in mental health distress among young people, he said, at the same time as funded mental health resources had become less available.

“That drives people towards medication because it’s accessible and it’s cheap,” he said.

“It often becomes the frontline treatment out of necessity rather than good clinical decision-making or what the evidence says works.”

Dr David Menkes, a Yale University-trained expert in psychological medicine, said the stretched system was not resourced to conduct adequate follow-up care in many cases.

“This is important because when these drugs are prescribed, especially to young people, they should be followed up within a week or two.

“Often patients with new prescriptions aren’t seen for months … That’s not good enough.”

Menkes described self-diagnosis through social media as “an absolute scourge”, saying platforms such as TikTok often encouraged people to incorrectly identify themselves as having mental health conditions.

While some people did find helpful information online, he believed the overall effect of exposure to social media was negative and contributed to the risks of overdiagnosis and overtreatment.

Better “mental health literacy” was needed, he said. While symptoms of anxiety and depression could signal illness, they were also often a normal part of growing up and everyday life.

MacDonald said evidence suggested social media was more likely to worsen mental health for young people who were already struggling, rather than cause mental illness itself.

Factors such as inequality, deprivation, trauma, violence in the home, family addiction and marginalisation were the main drivers of poor youth mental health, with social media playing a comparatively small role, he said.

For more on social media harm, follow the link below

Dr Prabani Wood, medical director at the Royal New Zealand College of General Practitioners, said a range of factors could be contributing to mental health challenges among younger people.

“They’ve lived through the lockdowns; their schooling was affected, and university was affected during the pandemic. These are formative years, and they went through a once-in-a-generation event,” Wood said.

“There’s also what’s happening in the world more broadly: uncertainty around global conflicts, artificial intelligence and jobs. All of that can create anxiety about the future.

“They’ve gone through a different process in life. Major stress during those formative years has probably played a part.”

She said young people who were prescribed antidepressants through fragmented care or repeat telehealth consultations could remain on medication for years without regular reviews.

While telehealth was an important tool, she said it could not replace the continuity of care that came from an ongoing relationship with a GP.

Greater awareness of mental health issues may also be leading more people to seek help, she said.

The symptoms people experienced were real, but she said social media may be playing a role in broader mental health trends.

“We know the negative effects of social media, and we’ve now got a whole generation of people growing up online. We’re probably seeing some of the effects of that on mental health,” Wood said.

Carla King, chair of the New Zealand Association of Counsellors’ school guidance counsellor advisory group, said antidepressants could be lifesaving, but prescribing them to young people was more complex because their brains were still developing.

King said it would be dangerous to dismiss all youth mental health concerns.

However, she said rising antidepressant prescription rates did not necessarily mean more students were struggling.

“It’s a sign that doctors are using the tools available to them in a mental health system that is not coping with the needs of our youth.”

King said access to effective therapeutic support remained limited, leaving school guidance counsellors to act as a frontline service for students in crisis.

“When a student presents as suicidal, we are required to refer them into that same system, which we know can’t properly support them. We often have to ask ourselves whether we’re doing more harm than good.”

She said the association was advocating for dedicated funding and a counsellor-to-student ratio of one counsellor for every 400 students.

“Right now, we’re firefighting.

“Students wait two to three weeks to see us. We’ve become the triage unit for a system that continues to not be properly resourced.”

Mental Health Minister Matt Doocey said the Government had invested in a range of youth mental health initiatives and was focused on reducing wait times and growing the workforce.

He said recent survey results suggested access to services was improving, although many young people still did not know where to seek help or felt too embarrassed to ask for support.

On antidepressant prescribing, Doocey said treatment decisions were made by qualified clinicians based on patients’ clinical needs, adding that rising use reflected a range of factors, including greater awareness of mental health issues and more people seeking help.

Bay of Plenty Regional Council to pause restructure of $3b-plus investment portfolio

New Zealand Herald July 18, 2026

Quayside Holdings is a council-controlled organisation that functions as the investment arm of the Bay of Plenty Regional Council, with a majority share in the Port of Tauranga. Photo / Local Democracy Reporting

Bay of Plenty Regional Council has confirmed plans are on hold to restructure its $3 billion-plus investment portfolio.

It comes after Local Government Minister Simon Watts wrote to the council on July 2 to “defer any decisions” relating to the fund’s restructure after being contacted by MPs and six mayors from the region.

Watts said councils should “exercise restraint” when making “significant, long-term decisions” relating to the ownership and governance of key regional assets until reform outcomes were clear.

Bay of Plenty Regional Council chairwoman Matemoana McDonald responded to Watts on Tuesday and confirmed the council will “follow the direction you have given us”.

“In terms of making any significant long-term decisions relating to investments, we will exercise restraint and do not intend to make further decisions until there is greater clarity on the arrangements that emerge from the reform processes,” her letter said.

The reforms could bring major change to the structure of councils in the region, with several merger options being considered.

McDonald said she would seek formal adoption at the next full council meeting “so that it is clear to all parties that this is our decision”.

The exchange came after the council ratified decisions on June 25 to enable the future restructuring of the fund, despite opposition from the mayors.

The council decided, after public consultation, to enable the portfolio to be restructured in the future by splitting different types of assets into separately managed entities.

It also agreed to explore options for partnering with an established community trust to hold the investments and for establishing a new charitable community trust.

This was done through an amendment to the council’s 2024-2034 Long-term Plan.

The fund is held by the council-controlled organisation (CCO) Quayside Holdings on behalf of the Bay of Plenty community.

Quayside manages it independently and provides an annual dividend to the council. Its primary holding is a majority (54.14%) share in the Port of Tauranga.

The Bay of Plenty Times has reported that three of Quayside’s seven directors are set to leave on September 30, while the resignation of a fourth – the regional council’s chief executive Fiona McTavish – came into effect on June 25.

McDonald wrote in her letter to Watts that the Long-term Plan Amendment had not established a new entity, not transferred assets nor would “predetermine any future structure”.

“Rather, it ensures that future options remain available, should they be considered appropriate once there is greater clarity regarding the future local government environment.”

McDonald said the council’s work in this area was driven by a “long-standing objective” to protect and enhance regional investment assets for current and future generations.

Work began in 2023 and formed part of the strategic direction adopted through the 2024-2034 Long-term Plan.

McDonald said it reflected the council’s continued approach to “prudent financial stewardship”, including protecting intergenerational assets and ensuring regional assets continued to support economic, environmental and community outcomes long-term.

She said the council prioritised having a “suitably qualified and experienced, majority independent” Quayside board.

This required regularly reviewing governance arrangements, director terms and establishing a cost-effective governance structure that continued to be fit for purpose, McDonald said.

Tauranga MP Sam Uffindell, who previously expressed his concerns to Watts about the fund’s restructure, said it was good to hear regional council had “pulled their heads in” and listened to the minister, local MPs and six mayors.

“I am still concerned that they walked down this path to begin with.

“Quayside is a highly successful independent investment entity, free from political interference and it needs to stay this way for the benefit of the Bay.”

Regional Development Minister Shane Jones contacted the Bay of Plenty Times on Tuesday, before the regional council responded to Watts, to speak about the restructure.

Jones said several people in Tauranga had raised “deep concerns” about Quayside’s future.

He was interested in Quayside’s future governance and referenced the Rangiuru Business Park, which received funding from Quayside and the Crown’s Provincial Growth Fund.

Jones said the Quayside fund should remain intact and the “handsome block of capital shouldn’t be turned into confetti”.

He was “deeply disturbed” by people’s fears that Quayside capital would “no longer be used economically” and instead suit councillors’ priorities, for example, “climate alarmism”.

Jones said his party, New Zealand First, rejected co-governance in a future model, including having “direct iwi appointments”.

On Thursday, Jones acknowledged the regional council had followed “the dictates of the Minister’s letter” but his co-governance and “climate alarmism” concerns remained.

Jones’ concerns were put to the regional council.

The regional council said Quayside continued to have a governance model with a majority of appointed independent directors.

“There are no plans to change this.”

Megan Wilson is a health and general news reporter for the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post. She has been a journalist since 2021.

Hawke’s Bay man calls for action on thermal paper receipts and plastic pollution

New Zealand Herald July 18, 2026

Havelock North resident Walter Breustedt is urging the Government to reduce unnecessary receipt printing, citing environmental concerns and the chemicals used in thermal receipts. Photo / Rafaella Melo

Many Kiwis already say “no receipt, thanks” at the checkout and a Havelock North man is calling on businesses and the Government to do it for them in a bid to help the environment.

Thermal receipts cannot be recycled and retired architect and engineer Walter Breustedt claims the chemicals used in printing them are also a potential health risk.

Breustedt has prepared a discussion paper he plans to take to the Ministry for the Environment and other relevant ministries after he meets Tukituki MP Catherine Wedd and Hastings councillor Callum Ross about the issue on July 31.

His paper calls on the Government to encourage businesses to reduce unnecessary receipt printing.

It also asks the Government to assess the overall health costs of plastic pollution, to review soft-plastic recycling, and to strengthen oversight of plastic and paper waste exports.

The Ministry for the Environment said it did not have a position on thermal paper receipts and was not considering any regulatory changes about receipt printing.

However, it noted many businesses already voluntarily offered customers the option of declining a printed receipt or choosing a digital one, describing those initiatives as “a good example” of retailers reducing their environmental impact.

For Breustedt, however, voluntary action does not go far enough.

He wants businesses to stop automatically printing thermal receipts.

“If you go to a cafe, they ask you, ‘do you need the receipt?’

“If you don’t, they take the receipt out of the Eftpos machine and throw it somewhere,” Breustedt said.

His discussion paper, supported by local church environmental groups, cited overseas studies suggesting thermal receipts contained chemicals such as bisphenol A (BPA) or bisphenol S (BPS) and that repeated exposure could pose health risks.

He claimed better protection was also needed for workers who handled receipts regularly.

Research cited in his paper suggested that while short exposure was unlikely to harm most people, it could be more concerning for pregnant women, children and those with thyroid issues.

Originally from Germany, Breustedt spent much of his career working on environmental projects and said he believed there was still much to be done in New Zealand.

“People believe when they are recycling plastic, it solves the problem,” he said.

“We have to reduce the amount of plastic that we are using.”

Breustedt said the aim was not to ban all receipts or all plastic overnight, but to push for practical changes and clearer information for the public.

He said he wanted people to be aware that recycling soft plastic into outdoor products could still lead to microplastic pollution in future.

Breustedt said he hoped the paper would start a wider conversation and ultimately lead to practical policy changes.

The Ministry for the Environment said reducing plastic pollution was a key focus through wider waste and resource efficiency programmes, including product stewardship schemes and previous bans on a range of hard-to-recycle and single-use plastic items.

“A third tranche of a work covering additional PVC and polystyrene food packaging phase-outs was to be in place by 2025, but this was put on hold pending further work and consultation with industry,” the ministry said.

“A Cabinet decision is expected in the coming months and, if approved, new regulations would likely take effect in 2030, aligning with similar moves anticipated in Europe.”

Hastings District Council’s waste planning manager Angela Atkins said thermal receipts were not accepted in kerbside recycling and that they should be placed in the rubbish bin.

“Where possible, residents can choose not to receive a printed receipt or request an electronic receipt instead,” she said.

The council encouraged businesses to reduce unnecessary waste where practical, including by using digital tools instead of printed materials where suitable.

“We recognise that the ability to offer electronic receipts may depend on the capabilities of individual point-of-sale systems,” Atkins said.

She said the council worked with businesses, households, schools and community groups to reduce waste through education, waste minimisation initiatives and support for more sustainable practices.

Inside Tairāwhiti Whenua Trust, New Zealand’s largest Māori farming collective

New Zealand Herald July 18, 2026

The Tairāwhiti Whenua Charitable Trust's 76 farms range in size from five to 46,000ha.

On the East Coast of the North Island, spread over 198,000ha, is Aotearoa’s largest collective of Māori farmland under the Tairāwhiti Whenua Charitable Trust. Olivia Caldwell reports what’s behind this farming community.

On coastal New Zealand between Gisborne and Wairoa are orchards, vineyards and thousands of stock units across 76 farms.

All owned by 140,000 shareholders.

“As you can imagine, there are always some heavy discussions,” says the chief executive of the Tairāwhiti Whenua Trust, Hilton Collier.

Without a doubt, any debate is outweighed by the employment the trust provides for the area, the people it houses and the produce it delivers.

The 76 farms range in size from five to 46,000ha.

Together, they employ more than 400 people, steward at least $738 million in assets, and generate over $51 million annually for the Tairāwhiti economy.

Established in 2023 in reaction to government-proposed RMA reforms, this large network of Māori landowners was formed to amplify the collective voice of the whenua and its people.

At a time when major regulatory shifts were reshaping land governance and environmental responsibilities, Tairāwhiti Māori landowners came together rather than being passive recipients of change.

“I guess what we’ve done is we put a formal structure and discipline around influencing macroeconomic policies,” Collier said.

“We knew how big we were.”

“Council didn’t know, so that’s when the lawyers arrived to the next meeting we had. And after that, we came to an understanding that decisions being made around the table would have a major impact on our operations, and we would defend it.”

The purpose was to ensure these Māori landholders were active in shaping the region’s future, he said.

“Māori land is a lot different to your typical mum and dad farmer in New Zealand.

“You’ve got a whole lot of beneficiaries, owners, shareholders, call them what you will.

“Ownership tends to be there through a lens of connection to place.”

Collier said communication had to be different, too.

When speaking to landowners, describing how decisions impact the land and its future often resonates more than economic arguments.

“It’s not just about making money for the sake of making money,” Collier said.

“I think giving people their cause or their purpose is fundamental to what we do.

“That purpose may be because they want to be a farmer of the year and be recognised for that.

“Others want to see career pathways for their children, grandchildren.”

Since 2023, the 198,000ha have seen change.

The trust’s research showed that the steep hill country and erosion-prone hills were redundant for farming. So it was planted out in native trees, or already existing trees were registered under the emissions trading scheme.

“The land feeds the people,” Collier said.

“So, if it’s not running sheep and cattle, it’s not creating a job; there is no reason why we can’t be using the emissions trading scheme to provide income.

“For how long now we’ve been told the emissions trading scheme is the death of farming?

“It’s the death of farming if farmers want to sell all their land to the highest bidder.

“We [Māori land owners] can’t sell land, so we’re looking at which parts of our state we put into ETS, because we quite like the idea of $50,000 a hectare worth of carbon.”

Instead of removing existing vegetation growing in the high country, the farmers have registered under the Emissions Trading Scheme and can earn $300 a hectare, ongoing.

“If you’re not making a return, get rid of it,” Collier said.

“Stop wasting money on it and redivert that investment into other parts of the farm, increase carrying capacity - we strip out costs.”

The newly native trees return around $1800 a hectare.

At the heart of the trust’s operation is the influence of the red meat sector, with 130,000ha still used for sheep and cattle.

The trust recently won the Gallagher Innovative Farming Award at the Beef + Lamb New Zealand Awards.

Māori and Pacific peoples form an important part of the red meat sector’s workforce, particularly among younger age groups, making them central to the sector’s future labour supply.

Around 25% of the sector are Māori and 11% Pacific peoples.

“We still have all those socio-economic problems; we’re not going to change it overnight,” Collier said.

“But if we start packaging things in a way that matters to our landowners that they can engage with, why wouldn’t they?”

Collier said much of the trust’s workforce was Māori; however, they employ the best people for the job.

“We invest in trading and upskill our people, whether those people come back to us or don’t, it doesn’t really matter.

“It’s about employing people in our region. And if they’re a good rugby player and they play for the family rugby club, that’s a bonus.”

Overall, the collective has increased farm revenue during its three years of operation, he said.

“A couple of 100 years ago, we probably went out for a hunt and ate whatever we killed,” Collier said.

“But today, it means using the land in a way that creates jobs, it creates enterprises, all those sorts of things.

“And then to be sustainable, not only do we need the jobs, we need somewhere to live, but we also need to make sure the land stays in place.

“That’s why I talk about feeding the whānau — because if we don’t continually look into the horizon and ask what that looks like, we’re going to wake up and we’ll still be producing black and white TVs when the world’s moved beyond colourful iPhones.”

South Taranaki farmers’ legacy still funding future vets and agricultural leaders 100 years on

New Zealand Herald July 18, 2026

Tikorangi sharemilker and Bashford-Nicholls scholarship recipient, Brent Stevenson.

Two South Taranaki farmers who left their farms in trust more than a century ago are still helping fund the next generation of agricultural and veterinary leaders.

Born in 1880, Claude William Nicholls and James Dawson Bashford were neighbours in rural South Taranaki, living just 5km apart.

In an era when it was common practice to leave a farm to family, they each chose a different path and established trusts so their land would continue benefiting their region long after they were gone.

Today, the Bashford-Nicholls Trust distributes about $300,000 annually in scholarships and awards supporting careers in agriculture and veterinary science.

One of the trust’s former scholarship recipients is Brent Stevenson, who sharemilks 1400 cows on a farm in Tikorangi, North Taranaki.

Growing up on a coastal Taranaki farm, Stevenson always had a connection to the land and an instinct for agriculture.

He received a Bashford-Nicholls Scholarship in 2007, 2008 and 2009 while completing a Bachelor of Applied Science in Rural Valuation and Management at Massey University in Palmerston North.

That financial support allowed him to focus on his studies and think seriously about the career he wanted to build.

After graduating, he worked across multiple regions of New Zealand, building relationships with farming families and rural businesses and gaining a first-hand understanding of their operations.

From 2010 to 2016, he brought that ground-level knowledge into a financial context at National Bank, helping farming clients navigate the business side of agriculture.

Eventually, Taranaki called him home, and today he farms in Tikorangi with his wife Amy and their two children.

Stevenson said he did not fully appreciate the scholarship’s value at the time.

“You’re just a student trying to get through, but that scholarship made a real difference.

“Everything I’ve built since, the farming, the relationships, coming home to Taranaki, it started there, studying in Palmy and having that support behind me.”

The trust continues to support students today.

One of them is Tayla Steele, who is in her fourth year of a Bachelor of Veterinary Science at Massey University in Palmerston North.

The Bashford-Nicholls Trust has supported her each year since she began her degree in 2023, helping to reduce her course fees.

But for Steele, the scholarship meant more than financial support.

“The scholarship gave me something that money can’t fully capture – time,” she said.

“Because a big chunk of my fees has been covered, I don’t have to spend any spare hours behind a checkout or working multiple jobs.

“Instead, I’ve been out on farms, in horse stables, and at desexing clinics, volunteering, getting my hands dirty, and turning everything I learn in the lecture theatre into real-world experience.

“That is the difference this trust has made. Not just a degree, but a vet in the making.”

With a year and a half until she graduates, Steele’s plan is clear: to return to Taranaki to build a career as a large-animal rural veterinarian, serving the communities that shaped her.

Steele is the first person in her family, across many generations, to attend university.

“The Bashford-Nicholls Trust didn’t just invest in my education,” she said.

“It invested in breaking a cycle, and I hope that means something to the next kid from Taranaki who wonders whether they can do it too.”

The trust’s reach extends far beyond a handful of scholarship recipients.

This year alone, it is supporting 66 undergraduate students, two master’s students and four PhD candidates pursuing careers in agriculture and veterinary science.

It also co-funds the Pivot Award in partnership with Massey University.

Last year, the Bashford-Nicholls Trust transferred $14 million in assets to Taranaki Foundation, marking the largest single transfer of trust assets in New Zealand’s community foundation network.

The transfer more than doubled Taranaki Foundation’s funds under management, from $13 million to $27 million.

The trust continues to operate as its own entity, focused on supporting rural students and agricultural innovation, while Taranaki Foundation provides investment management and community support.

Taranaki Foundation chief executive Josh Hickford said the legacy created by Nicholls and Bashford would continue to benefit future generations.

“Our children, and their children, will still be telling this story. That’s what we’re here to protect and grow.”

Sweet Caroline won’t last forever: What’s New Zealand’s next sporting anthem? Glenn Dwight

New Zealand Herald July 18, 2026

So good! So good! So good! Photo / Photosport

Before I start, a quick disclaimer.

This article was written before last night’s All Blacks test against Ireland, so by the time you read it, parts of it may have aged about as well as the chicken fried rice that’s been in the fridge a week.

Having said that, it still passes the sniff test.

Anyway, back to the story …

Last Saturday, I was watching the All Blacks test in Wellington, and I witnessed something I don’t normally associate with an All Blacks crowd.

They looked like they were having fun.

Now I know that sounds like a strange thing to notice at a rugby game, but hear me out.

Normally, when the television cameras pan across an All Blacks crowd, everyone looks like they’re being held against their will at a compulsory workplace team-building day.

You know the sort of thing.

HR has promised it’ll be “fun”, but deep down, everyone knows they’re only there because attendance was strongly encouraged in the office-wide email.

There are polite smiles and awkward applause. And if the designated radio station rolls out one of its “Come on, everyone!” moments, every Kiwi immediately adopts the same strategy.

Don’t make eye contact. Not with the MC, not with the camera, and certainly not with the person you came to the game with.

Suddenly, it’s the perfect time to top up the beer tray or see if the toilet queue has shortened.

Then the kiss cam appears on the big screen.

Like Halloween, it’s an American tradition we’ve somehow embraced despite nobody being entirely sure why. Thankfully, Coldplay may have finally retired that particular tradition.

And please don’t get me started on the Mexican wave.

But Wellington felt different.

There was singing.

There was cheering.

People were actually having fun.

There was even what could only be described as mild enthusiasm for the halftime entertainment, which is about as rare at a rugby test as finding a car park within walking distance of the stadium.

Mind you, choosing halftime entertainment is a bit like organising a potluck dinner.

Everyone reckons they know what people want, but no matter what you serve, someone will complain.

For me, halftime entertainment peaked back in the Athletic Park days, when Wellington crowds enjoyed kite-flying.

I never saw it myself, but Newstalk ZB sports commentator Ross Bond tells the stories with such enthusiasm you start wondering why we’ve spent the past 40 years trying to improve on perfection.

And to me, there’s nothing wrong with a marching troupe.

Twenty people walking in perfect formation while someone enthusiastically twirls a baton.

It’s wholesome, it’s impressive, and nobody has to kiss a complete stranger or your HR manager on the big screen.

But if we really want to compete with the Americans, let’s stop mucking around altogether and go full Super Bowl.

Fireworks. Drones. A fighter jet flyover. Lorde descending from the stadium roof singing Slice of Heaven while Richie McCaw arrives by jet boat ... only to suffer a very unfortunate Adidas wardrobe malfunction.

Think There’s Something About Mary.

But the half-time show wasn’t what got the crowd going.

That honour belonged to the oldest trick in the stadium entertainment handbook.

Sweet Caroline.

“So good ...”

“So good ...”

“So good ...”

Thirty-five thousand people instantly became the world’s least rehearsed choir.

And that’s what made me smile.

Usually, the only crowd I associate with that sort of atmosphere and enthusiasm is Warriors supporters.

They could turn a queue at the supermarket into the sort of party the Beastie Boys fought for the right to attend.

Up the Wahs.

Which got me thinking.

One day, Sweet Caroline is going to become not so sweet anymore.

So we need a succession plan, and New Zealand needs to find its own sporting anthem.

Other countries have already nailed it.

Ireland has Zombie.

Scotland has Flower of Scotland.

And the Welsh ... well, I’m convinced you could hand them the ingredients list from a packet of vegan sausages and by the second verse 40,000 people would be in tears.

Now, before anyone from the Alternative Commentary Collective emails me, yes, I know the obvious choice for New Zealand’s unofficial official national anthem is Sandstorm.

To be fair, it ticks a lot of boxes.

The lyrics are achievable.

“Doo doo doo doo ...”

But I think we can do better.

If New Zealand is going to have its own sporting singalong, it needs to be a proper ding-dong.

For those unfamiliar with the official sporting scale, that sits comfortably above a humdinger and well clear of a doozy.

Which is where the argument begins.

Let’s start with the obvious.

Dave Dobbyn’s Loyal would be a strong contender, although for many of us it still carries the emotional baggage of the 2013 America’s Cup campaign.

As a nation, we flew Sir Dave to San Francisco to sing Loyal as Dean Barker looked set to lift the Cup ... only for Jimmy to spit on our parade.

Poi E would be difficult to argue against.

It has been bringing New Zealanders together for decades, regardless of age, background or whether you have ever successfully used a poi.

The only concern is the risk of widespread poi entanglement among the less co-ordinated members of the crowd. I put my hand up here.

Then there is Bliss.

An outstanding song and a proven Kiwi singalong, but perhaps not the easiest choice in the current climate.

Before kickoff, the stadium announcer would need to deliver a responsible drinking message, a health warning and possibly confirm that nobody was legally required to follow the instructions in the chorus.

Finally, there’s Why Does Love Do This To Me?

Brilliant song, although asking 40,000 rugby supporters to publicly discuss their feelings feels optimistic.

And maybe that’s what struck me most about Wellington, they watched the game with feeling. Showing their feelings.

Because that’s what live sport should be.

Not 80 minutes of sitting quietly analysing the breakdown.

It’s supposed to be noisy. It’s supposed to be fun.

It’s supposed to leave you with a sore throat because you spent the night cheering.

Whether Neil Diamond remains our adopted sporting anthem or somebody eventually writes a Kiwi singalong of our own doesn’t really matter.

What Wellington showed us is that it is okay to enjoy sport.

Although if someone could organise the return of halftime kite flying, I wouldn’t complain.

So good.

So good.

So good.

Kem Ormond’s vegetable garden: Growing Brussels sprouts takes patience, but it’s worth it

New Zealand Herald July 18, 2026

To grow Brussels sprouts, all you need is patience, determination and a will to succeed. Photo / 123rf

Thought I would sow a seed: have you ever considered growing your own Brussels sprouts – or are you not fussed on them?

They are a vegetable that people seem to love or hate; there seems to be no in-between.

Freshly picked and cooked Brussels sprouts can be used in so many ways.

Cooked, then lightly browned in a fry pan with butter and some slivered almonds, sliced in a sprout slaw, used with pasta, charred on the barbecue, they are delicious with crispy pieces of bacon.

In fact, you can use them as you would cabbage.

Now for the hard part: to successfully grow them.

You need patience, determination and a will to succeed.

You can grow Brussels sprouts from seeds or seedlings.

Your soil needs to be well-composted, aiming for a firmer bed rather than a fluffy one. Brussels sprouts need a good footing.

They like to be in full sun as it builds strong stems and tight sprouts.

The ideal time to plant your seedlings is late summer into early autumn, so the plants can mature through winter and into spring.

The colder weather seems to add to the flavour and deter the bitterness that can sometimes happen.

As the seedlings grow and the stalk starts to get bigger, add some stakes that the sprouts can be gently tied to.

This will keep the roots from being disturbed and moving around.

Consistent moisture and regular feeding are key.

Over the summer, make sure you deep water and mulch to assist with keeping the roots cool, so the plant doesn’t bolt.

Sprouts are hungry feeders. If you find the leaves are not as green as they were, then they probably need feeding.

I know people find sprouts hard to grow, and this is because the plants dislike stress – they don’t like wind, need regular feeding and watering – and you need to keep an eye out for pests.

They are like the prima donnas of the brassica family, really!

You know they are ready to be harvested when the sprouts feel firm and tight. You start harvesting from the bottom and make your way up.

Growing Brussels sprouts can be a challenge, and I won’t deny it.

However, that is exactly what makes vegetable gardening so satisfying.

When you finally succeed in growing a crop that has tested your patience and skill, the reward is more than worth the effort.

Tasting the harvest at the end of the season brings a real sense of achievement and makes all the hard work worthwhile.

Kem Ormond is a features writer for The Country. She’s also a keen gardener.

Pastures Past: Learning by correspondence in 1931 and 1947

New Zealand Herald July 18, 2026

Correspondence schooling was delivered through the post. Photo / Duncan Brown

Kem Ormond takes a look at the world of farming back in the day.

In this week’s Pastures Past, she’s found newspaper articles from 1931 and 1947 on correspondence schools.

Correspondence schooling hasn’t disappeared; it’s just modernised, with most learning now taking place online rather than through the post.

Families may choose correspondence schooling because they live in a remote area far from a suitable school, travel frequently, live overseas, have health, social or special learning needs, or are being homeschooled.

Back in 1947, however, many children turned to correspondence lessons for a very different reason.

A major polio epidemic led to school closures and restrictions on children gathering in public places.

In many parts of the North Island, schools remained closed for months, with many children learning from home through correspondence lessons and radio broadcasts.

Below is a selection of historical stories from the NZ Herald (1931) and the Gisborne Herald.

Closing small schools

Few in Auckland District.

Correspondence tuition

New Zealand Herald, December 8, 1931

Only a very small number of schools in the Auckland Education Board’s district will be affected by the Education Department’s proposal to close small schools of the Grade 0 standard.

The chairman of the board, Mr. A. Burns, stated yesterday that only four schools were likely to come under the correspondence tuition system, which would be substituted for teachers.

If the change were approved it would come into force at the beginning of the next school year in February.

Mr. Burns said that in normal years, grade 0 schools, which were those back-block schools with an average attendance of less than nine pupils, were taught by uncertificated teachers, who were paid £15 a pupil and provided by the parents with board.

In some cases their wages were increased by parents’ subsidies.

Schools with more than nine pupils were staffed with salaried teachers in the board’s employ.

In all, there were 14 grade 0 schools in the province, and of those, ten had from four to seven pupils.

Those would not be affected, but the board had invited the parents of children at the four other schools to come under the correspondence system.

Replies had not yet been received by the board.

It was not anticipated that any action would be necessary with regard to the larger grade 0 schools.

Mr. Burns added that the department claimed that good results had been obtained in most cases from correspondence tuition, although there were certain difficulties.

In the isolated areas where the schools were situated, mails were not delivered regularly.

Some parents were unable through pressure of farming or domestic duties to supervise the children’s work, and others were possibly not competent to do so.

At the same time, the children lost the teacher’s influence in building up character, there being no personal touch in the teaching.

Notwithstanding those drawbacks, however, the results of correspondence tuition in the past in other isolated parts, such as lighthouses, had been very satisfactory.

Correspondence work

Possibility next year

Gisborne Herald, December 13, 1947

If the schools do not re-open on the normal date, sole teachers in country schools will prepare their own correspondence schools and in other schools, correspondence courses will have to be conducted through the press, stated the senior inspector, Mr A. H. Denne, at yesterday’s meeting of the Hawke’s Bay Education Board at Napier.

A recommendation to the Education Department that it should see that all schools receive some form of treatment before children return to school, to prevent infection is to be forwarded to the department by the board, on the suggestion of Mr J. T. Hill.

His original suggestion was that the schools should be fumigated, but it was decided that the method of treatment should be left to the department.

Members of the board considered that the department could either carry out the suggestion itself or make grants to school committees for the purpose.

- Source: Papers Past

Please just give us ferries that work and spare us the politics – Editorial

New Zealand Herald July 18, 2026

Minister for Rail Winston Peters used the naming of the new ferries as an opportunity to play politics. Photo / Mark Mitchell

What a saga it has been replacing our ageing Interislander ferries.

The latest episode came on Friday when Winston Peters, the Minister for Rail, announced the names of the ferries – Kupe and Cook.

That really should’ve been the end of the matter, but the NZ First leader used the opportunity to play politics and send forth a barrage of fighting words to anyone who might criticise the names.

“Now, we know exactly what will happen,” Peters said.

“The snivelling wokesters will work themselves into a lather over the name Cook, while offering only passing approval for Kupe. That is how shallow this has become.

“It is fashionable now in certain circles to treat Captain Cook as nothing more than a symbol to be condemned, cancelled, and cast out. A harbinger of colonisation, they say. A figure of division, they say. A relic to be erased.”

While social media was probably awash with nonsensical reckons this weekend about what the ferries were named, and how woke or not they are, middle New Zealand must be tired of this.

This country is in a giant infrastructure hole.

New Zealand’s infrastructure deficit is estimated at more than $200 billion, and the New Zealand Infrastructure Commission projects that we need $1 trillion over the next 30 years just to play catch-up with population growth.

Our current Interislander fleet has been an issue for years and has had several embarrassing incidents, most notably in June 2024 when the Aratere ferry ran aground shortly after departing Picton.

Kiwis and businesses who rely on this service to traverse Cook Strait will care little about what the ferries are named and whether wokesters will work themselves into a lather. What they care about and what they need is reliability.

Our economy is small and demands we have an effective bridge across the water separating our two major islands and populations. These ferries, above anything else, must simply work.

We should also be much closer to having new ferries than we are.

Labour Party transport spokesman Tangi Utikere said the announcement on Friday was “another sideshow”.

“If Nicola Willis hadn’t destroyed Labour’s iReX programme, New Zealand would be preparing to welcome modern replacement ferries into service.

“Instead, they’ve wasted years, wasted hundreds of millions of dollars, and pushed replacement and resilience even further into the future.”

But Labour has also played its part in this shemozzle by failing to control the costs of the initial project.

The Government cancelled the previous iReX mega-ferry project after costs ballooned to nearly $3b.

Last year, the long-awaited contract was signed nearly two years later, while the termination of the initial contract with iReX shipbuilder Hyundai Mipo Dockyard cost taxpayers $144 million in break fees.

The new ferries are said to have about a three-decade lifespan and, more importantly, Peters confirmed during his announcement on Friday that KiwiRail would continue to own the ferries once they arrive.

The Government had previously refused to commit to full KiwiRail ownership.

Peters also announced that KiwiRail would pay port fees to CentrePort in Wellington and the Port of Marlborough, at a commercial price, which would allow the ports to earn a “reasonable profit” on their combined $210m investment in infrastructure to accommodate the ferries.

These are the important details, not what the names of the boats are ... unless, of course, a poll is held and we the public decide it should be Boaty McBoatface.
